title: How does a ring buffer reuse storage?
answer: Values stay in their slots while head and tail move, and both wrap back to slot 0 to reuse freed slots

checks.question: Carry on from the last step of “Push 5, pop 2, push 2”, where head and tail are both at slot 2. Pop three times, then push 8. Which values leave, which slot takes 8, and in what order do the rest come out?
checks.answer: The pops return 3, 4, 5, and head wraps to slot 0. Tail is still at slot 2, so 8 goes there. Reading from head gives 6, 7, 8: the order comes from head, not from the slot numbers.

checks.question: A ring of eight slots takes eight pushes and then eight pops. Where are head and tail, and how does the ring know it is empty?
checks.answer: Both are at slot 0, just where they were when it was full (head 0, tail 0). Only length, 0 now against 8 then, tells empty from full.

checks.question: A queue of 1,000 values is drained by 1,000 pops. How many value copies does the array queue make in all, and how many does the ring make?
checks.answer: The array makes 499,500: each pop copies every value still behind the front, 999, then 998, down to 0. The ring makes none, because a pop moves only head.

steps.title: A queue in an array: each pop moves every value left
steps.line: Predict: how could pop take 1 without moving the other 4?
steps.caption: The simplest queue keeps its values in order in an array. Push writes at the end; pop takes the front, then copies every other value one slot left, as the language’s definition of Array.prototype.shift does. Popping from five values moves 4; from a thousand, 999. Engines may store some arrays differently, but these are the copies the definition describes. The order stays right because every pop pays for every value left behind.
steps.picture: 1. slot 0. 2. slot 1. 3. slot 2. 4. slot 3. 5. slot 4. 2. 3. 4. 5. empty. pop() returned 1 and moved 4 values.

steps.title: Answer: keep the values still, and move two markers instead
steps.line: Predict: after five pushes, where are head and tail?
steps.caption: Keep five fixed slots and remember two positions: head, the slot pop reads next, and tail, the slot push writes next. Push writes at tail and moves tail on; pop reads at head and moves head on. Values stay in their slots while head and tail move, and both wrap back to slot 0 to reuse freed slots. Queue order starts at head, not at the leftmost or lowest-numbered slot. The three fields start at 0.

steps.title: Answer: both back at slot 0, so only length says full
steps.line: Predict: pop twice. Which values leave, and does anything move?
steps.caption: Each push outlines the slot at tail, copies v into it, then moves tail on modulo five and adds one to length. After five pushes tail has wrapped to 0, where head is, just as when the ring was empty; only length, 5, says the ring is full. Coincident markers cannot distinguish “nothing to read” from “no room to write”.

steps.title: Answer: 1 and 2 leave, and no other value moves
steps.line: Predict: tail is at 0. Where do push 6 and push 7 go?
steps.caption: Each pop copies the value at head out to the tray, clears its slot and moves head on: 1 from slot 0, then 2 from slot 1, and head is at 2. The array queue would have moved 4 values and then 3; the ring moved none. Tail is still at 0, the first of the two outlined slots the pops freed.

steps.title: Answer: into slots 0 and 1, the slots the pops freed
steps.caption: Tail wrapped to 0 after the fifth push, so 6 and 7 are copied into slots 0 and 1, the storage two pops gave back, and no stored value moves. Length is back to 5, with head and tail both at 2. Left to right the slots hold 6, 7, 3, 4, 5, but the queue starts at head and wraps past slot 4, so the markers decide the order, not the slot numbers.

steps.line: The first line of push finds length === capacity, both 5.
steps.caption: push checks length === capacity on its first line, so with length 5 it throws Full before writing a slot or moving either marker. The 6 is crossed out short of slot 0 and goes to the refused tray, and head, tail and length do not change.

steps.title: push 7 is refused too, and the ring is unchanged
steps.line: Head, tail and length still read 0, 0 and 5.
steps.caption: push 7 is refused the same way and joins 6 in the refused tray; the ring still holds 1 to 5. Some ring buffers overwrite the oldest value instead. This one refuses, so no stored value is lost and the caller must handle Full.
